content.value: Think of Git as a supercharged 'Time Machine' for your code. Every time you make a checkpoint (called a **commit**), Git saves a snapshot of your entire project.

If you break something, you can easily travel back to any previous snapshot. It also lets multiple software engineers work on the exact same project simultaneously without overwriting each other's work.
Git vs GitHub: Git is the command-line tool running on your computer. GitHub is a cloud website (like Google Drive for code) that hosts Git repositories.

content.title: First Time Setup
content.value:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
git init                     # Turn current folder into a Git repository
git status                   # Check what files have changed

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between Git and GitHub?
options: They are the exact same product
Git is the local version control tool; GitHub is a cloud hosting service for Git repos
Git is for Python; GitHub is for JavaScript
GitHub runs on your laptop; Git is a website
quiz.explanation: Git is the underlying tool that tracks file changes locally. GitHub is a cloud platform for storing and sharing Git repositories online.

content.value: A **branch** is like a parallel universe for your project. The main production code lives on the `main` branch. When building a new feature, you create a feature branch so you don't break working code.

content.title: Branching Commands
content.value:
git branch feature-login        # Create a new branch
git checkout feature-login      # Switch to feature-login branch
git checkout -b feature-login   # Shortcut: create AND switch in one step
git checkout main               # Switch back to main branch
git merge feature-login         # Combine feature-login code INTO main
Merge vs Rebase (Top Interview Question!): Merge preserves full history and creates a 'merge commit'. Rebase moves your feature branch commits onto the tip of main for a clean linear history.

quiz.question: Why do developers create feature branches instead of committing directly to main?
options: To make the code run faster
To keep working production code safe while developing new features separately
Because Git requires at least 5 branches
quiz.explanation: Feature branches isolate experimental or incomplete work from the stable main codebase until the feature is tested and ready to merge.
